doc.title: Dave Rivello interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012

title: The Basie band, Brookmeyer's thrill and why it swung
summary: Rivello praises Basie's Chairman of the Board, relates Brookmeyer's one night with Basie, and says constant touring built the band's feel.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: Okay. What about something classic? “Shiny Stockings” or those kind of things. Is that a different — I can’t finish the question really but, it’s another era.

I think understanding that part of things is important. And I believe that anything that the Count Basie Orchestra did, I think you have to just know that. You have to be able to feel that. You have to have listened to it so much that it’s part of you. And my favorite, probably, Count Basie album is “Chairman of the Board.” And Thad Jones wrote some of the arrangements and Frank Foster’s — I think it’s Frank Foster — “Blues in Hoss Flat,” and that’s one of the best things ever. And lots of people know that because it was in the Jerry Lewis movie, you know, “The Nutty Professor” or “The Absent-Minded Professor,” whichever one it was with the black and white. But yeah, I think that even a guy that was as progressive as Bob Brookmeyer was, the biggest thrill in his life that he talked about was he played once with Basie’s band. And he said like the thrill in his body was never matched with any drugs, anything ever, the rest of his life. And that was, you know, he grew up in Kansas City, he was like a teenager then. And he lived to eighty, almost eighty-two years old, and nothing matched that feeling. So that was in him no matter if he

wrote very strange modern classical music — what people would term strange — but I mean very avante garde, still somehow Basie was in there. And I think that that feeling and that band has to go with anybody who’s serious about this music.
Do you have an opinion on how they achieved that, especially with the Great American Rhythm Section?

I think a lot of it had to do with — those guys just lived together, and they played every night on the road. And I think they knew one another and they trusted one another, and it’s something that we can’t really have now, because there aren’t bands that are playing that much. I mean some of those gigs were supposedly six and eight hours long with the Basie band. They were just playing all night. And in the morning they’d leave the club and then they’d come back in the afternoon again and then play all through the night. And you know there were times off where other bands would play on an opposite stage, but still, they were playing so much, it was their life. And I don’t know that we can really get back to that. But I think that’s a lot of why it felt so good.
